title: The Law
summary: Madame Danglars begs Villefort to go easy on Andrea Cavalcanti, now exposed as the escaped convict Benedetto, to spare her family more scandal. Villefort, haunted by the deaths in his own house, refuses, and news comes that Benedetto has been arrested.
details: After the disastrous contract-signing, Madame Danglars hurries, veiled, to the rooms of her lover Lucien Debray. He is out at his club, where friends are teasing him that he ought to marry Eugénie and her two millions himself. She waits until nearly midnight and goes home. The maid says Eugénie and Mademoiselle d'Armilly went to their room together, so she suspects nothing of their flight. Lying awake, she realizes how deep the disgrace is, and remembers that she felt no pity when Mercédès was struck by a similar blow.

She decides only Villefort can help, and plans to appeal to their old intimacy. Next morning she drives to his house, which now looks like a plague hospital: the porter suspects every visitor, and neighbours wonder aloud whether there will be another funeral today. Villefort receives her with a grief-stricken calm. She asks him to let “the impostor” escape, or at least to delay the trial. He corrects her: Andrea Cavalcanti, really Benedetto, is an assassin, a Corsican of unknown parents who was sent to the galleys (prison labour) at sixteen for forgery.

Villefort guesses what she is thinking: that people say the deaths in his house were not natural. Before a crucifix he swears that whoever the culprits are, they will die. In a bitter outburst he admits he has sinned, perhaps more deeply than others, and says every criminal he condemns proves he is not the only wicked man. A despatch arrives: Benedetto has been taken at Compiègne. Madame Danglars leaves, pale, and Villefort gloats that a murder case will make a splendid session of the assizes (the criminal court).

title: The Apparition
summary: As Valentine slowly recovers, a man steps through her library door one night. It is the Count of Monte Cristo, who has been watching her from the house next door and swapping her poisoned drinks for safe ones. He tells her to pretend to sleep and see who comes.
details: Valentine is still weak and feverish. Her stepmother tells her about Eugénie's flight and Benedetto's arrest, but she hardly takes it in. By day Noirtier sits with her. In the evening Dr. d'Avrigny brings her night draught himself, and a nurse watches until she sleeps. Then the keys go to Villefort, so her room can only be reached through the rooms of Madame de Villefort and little Edward. Every morning Morrel gets news from Noirtier. Monte Cristo promised him that if Valentine lived two hours she would be saved, and four days have now passed.

At night Valentine is haunted by fevered visions. One night after eleven she sees the library door open without a sound and a man come towards her bed. When she reaches for her glass he stops her hand. He holds the glass up to the lamp, tastes a spoonful, and says in a living voice, “Now you may drink.” She recognizes the Count of Monte Cristo.

The count says he has rented the next house and has watched for four sleepless nights from behind the hidden door. Whenever her drink was dangerous, he replaced the poison with a healthy draught. He is keeping her alive for Maximilian, who has told him everything. He explains that the Saint-Mérans and Barrois were poisoned. Noirtier's long medical treatment protected him, and Noirtier has been protecting Valentine too, by making her share his bitter-tasting drinks. But a much stronger dose four days ago would have killed her. The count has seen the poisoner. Instead of naming them, he tells her to pretend to sleep and watch at midnight, then slips back behind the door.

title: Locusta
summary: Pretending to sleep, Valentine watches her stepmother, Madame de Villefort, pour poison into her glass. The count explains the motive, Valentine's fortune passing to little Edward, and gives her a pill, telling her to fear nothing even if she wakes in a tomb.
details: The title refers to Locusta, a notorious poisoner of ancient Rome. Valentine waits, terrified. At half past midnight she hears the count scratch softly at the library door. Then the other door, the one from Edward's room, opens. Someone whispers her name twice, and she keeps breathing evenly. Peeping out, she sees a woman in a white dressing-gown emptying a phial into her glass. It is Madame de Villefort. Valentine's shudder makes her stepmother freeze and watch, but at last she empties the phial and slips away.

The count returns and tastes the drink. It is no longer brucine but a strong narcotic that would have killed her. He explains why: Valentine has 200,000 livres a year. If she dies, her father inherits, and after him his only son, Edward. That is why the Saint-Mérans died, and why Noirtier was targeted once he made Valentine his heir. He reminds her of a man in a brown cloak at Perugia whom her stepmother questioned about aqua tofana, a famous poison. Valentine would rather die than denounce her stepmother, and she worries the crimes will fall on Edward. The count says her father is not involved, though he should have been the one protecting her.

The count asks her to trust him blindly and to tell no one, not even her father. Whatever happens, even if she loses consciousness or wakes in a vault or a coffin, she must not be afraid. Thinking of Maximilian, she swallows a pea-sized pill from his little emerald box and falls asleep. He pours most of the poisoned drink into the fireplace so that it will look as if she drank it, and leaves.

title: Valentine
summary: Before dawn Madame de Villefort finds Valentine cold and still. In the morning the nurse raises the alarm, Dr. d'Avrigny pronounces Valentine dead and finds poison in her glass, the servants flee, and Maximilian arrives in time to hear the word “Dead!”
details: At about half past four, Madame de Villefort creeps in to see what her drink has done. She throws what is left in the glass into the ashes, then rinses and replaces the glass. Valentine is not breathing, her heart feels cold and motionless, and her nails are turning blue. The poisoner stands frozen by the bed, caught between fascination and remorse, until the lamp flickers out and she gropes her way back to her room.

The nurse comes at dawn, thinks Valentine is asleep, and dozes in an armchair. At eight she notices the stiff arm and screams. D'Avrigny and Villefort rush up, and the doctor declares that Valentine is dead. Villefort collapses at the bedside, and the servants all run from the “accursed house.”

Madame de Villefort arrives and forces out a few tears. Then she sees d'Avrigny studying the glass, which is somehow a third full again with the same coloured liquid she is sure she threw away. The doctor tastes it and says it is no longer brucine. A drop of nitric acid turns it blood-red. She staggers out and faints in her room. Only d'Avrigny sees her go, and he sends the nurse to help her.

Meanwhile Morrel comes to Noirtier's door as usual and finds the house empty and silent. Noirtier's terrified eyes tell him something has happened to Valentine. Morrel runs upstairs and hears d'Avrigny and Villefort say, “Dead!”

title: Maximilian
summary: Maximilian carries Noirtier to Valentine's deathbed, declares himself her betrothed, and demands justice. Noirtier privately reveals the killer to Villefort, who swears a terrible revenge within three days if the secret is kept. An Italian abbé from next door watches over the body.
details: Villefort orders the stranger out. Morrel leaves, but minutes later he carries Noirtier, chair and all, up the stairs with almost superhuman strength. Calling Noirtier “my father,” he begs him to tell them that he was Valentine's betrothed, and the old man weeps. Villefort knew nothing of the engagement. He forgives Morrel and tells him to say his last farewell.

Morrel refuses: Valentine needs an avenger, not just a priest. This is the fourth victim in four months, he says. He overheard Villefort and d'Avrigny in the garden the night Madame de Saint-Méran died, and he denounces the crime to the procureur du roi (the king's prosecutor). D'Avrigny joins him, ashamed that his silence encouraged the murderer. Noirtier signals that he knows the killer and asks to be left alone with Villefort.

A quarter of an hour later Villefort comes back livid, holding the shreds of a quill pen. He begs both men to keep the secret. Within three days, he promises, his revenge will make the boldest heart tremble, and Noirtier confirms it. D'Avrigny agrees. Morrel kisses Valentine's cold lips and rushes out in despair.

With the servants gone, d'Avrigny handles the formalities and brings the “doctor of the dead,” the official who certifies deaths, who confirms it. Villefort asks for the nearest priest, an Italian abbé who lives next door. The abbé already knows Valentine's name and has prayed for her. When Noirtier meets his eyes, he seems to read something there. Once he is alone, the abbé bolts the doors, including the one to Madame de Villefort's room.

title: Danglars’ Signature
summary: On the morning of Valentine's funeral, the count calls on Danglars and walks off with five million francs in bonds that the banker owed to the hospitals' charity fund. Unable to pay the charities, Danglars quietly prepares to flee France.
details: The Abbé Busoni watched over Valentine's body until daybreak. Noirtier is found sleeping almost peacefully, which surprises d'Avrigny and Villefort. Villefort, who has not slept, buries himself in writing the indictment against Benedetto and leaves the funeral reception to a colourless cousin. Debray, Château-Renaud and Beauchamp gossip among the mourners. Beauchamp's paper has hinted that if four deaths had happened in anyone else's house, Villefort would have looked into them more closely. They notice that the count and Morrel are missing.

The count has gone to see Danglars. The banker complains about the year's misfortunes: Morcerf dishonoured and dead, himself made ridiculous by Benedetto, and Eugénie gone abroad. The count flatters his vast wealth. Danglars proudly shows him five bonds of a million francs each, payable on sight at the Bank of France. The count is still owed 5,100,000 francs on his credit, so he pockets the bonds and hands over a receipt he wrote in advance. Danglars panics, because the money was meant for the charity fund, but he cannot refuse without admitting weakness.

M. de Boville, now Receiver-General of the charities (the official who collects funds for the hospitals), arrives for the five million. Danglars shows him the count's receipt, drawn on Thomson & French of Rome, and asks him to come back tomorrow at noon. Boville mentions that Mercédès and Albert have given their whole fortune to the hospitals rather than keep money “so guiltily acquired.” Danglars claims Eugénie has gone to a strict convent with a nun. Once Boville leaves, Danglars calls him a fool, pockets the receipt, gathers about 50,000 francs, burns some papers, writes a letter to his wife, and checks that his passport is still valid.

title: The Cemetery of Père-Lachaise
summary: At Valentine's funeral the count keeps his eyes on Maximilian, follows him home, and stops him from shooting himself by revealing that he is Edmond Dantès, the Morrel family's secret benefactor. He makes Maximilian promise to live one more month.
details: Valentine is buried at Père-Lachaise in a vault marked “The families of Saint-Méran and Villefort,” as her mother Renée had wished, and a huge crowd follows the coffin. The count arrives and searches anxiously for Morrel, then spots him slipping between the yew trees. Twice he checks whether Morrel is carrying a weapon. After the speeches, the count hides behind a tomb as Morrel kneels at the grave and murmurs, “Oh, Valentine!” Morrel calmly turns down a ride and walks home to the Rue Meslay, and the count follows.

Julie, watching Penelon graft roses in the garden, greets the count happily. Upstairs Morrel's door is locked, so the count smashes its glass panel with his elbow and pretends he slipped. He sees the pistols and the letter Morrel was writing, and accuses him of planning suicide. Morrel furiously blames the count for his false promises. The count replies that he alone has the right to forbid it: he saved Morrel's father, sent the purse and the Pharaon, and he is the Edmond Dantès who once held little Maximilian on his knees.

Morrel calls Julie and Emmanuel. The count stops him before he can say the name, but they embrace the count as their unknown benefactor, and Julie fetches the treasured silk purse. The count says he will leave France within a week.

Alone with Morrel, the count urges him to hope. Morrel makes him promise that if he is not cured in a month, on 5 October, the count will give him pistols and a painless poison. It is 5 September, ten years to the day since the count saved Morrel's father. Morrel swears not to harm himself before then and agrees to live with the count. Haydée, the count says, left last night to wait for him.

title: Dividing the Proceeds
summary: Madame Danglars learns that her husband has fled, and Debray coldly hands over her share of their stock-market profits and drops her. Upstairs in the same plain house, Mercédès and Albert, now poor, plan their futures: she will go to Marseilles, and he has enlisted as a soldier in Africa.
details: Debray keeps a secret apartment in the Rue Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where a veiled lady visits him. The morning after the count's visit to Danglars, Madame Danglars rushes there: her husband left last night. His mocking letter says he paid out five million and is running from a second demand. He suspects she has hidden away much of his fortune, and he leaves her “as I took you,—rich, but little respected.”

She hopes Debray will now stand by her. Instead he coolly advises her to travel, then settles their partnership. From her stake of 100,000 francs, their speculations since April have made 2,400,000, and he hands her 1,340,000 in notes, bonds and a cheque. She waits in vain for one kind word, then leaves without saying goodbye. Debray, keeping 1,060,000 francs for himself, reflects that he would have married Valentine had she lived.

In a bare room upstairs live Mercédès and Albert, who moved here after giving up their fortune. Mercédès has lost her spark, and Albert tells her they have no money. His plan: she will go to the little house in the Allées de Meilhan in Marseilles, where 3,000 francs are buried in the garden. He has sold his watch and signed up for the Spahis (French cavalry serving in Africa) as a paid substitute for another man, for 2,000 francs, half paid now. He means to earn a name of his own. In six months he will be an officer, or dead.

On the stairs they run into Debray. Albert introduces him as “once a friend” and politely refuses his help. Debray, with a million in his pocket, is shaken by the contrast between the two women. Next day Mercédès leaves by coach. From a window at Lafitte's bank, a hidden man watches and asks God how he can restore the happiness he has taken from these innocent people.

title: The Lions’ Den
summary: In La Force prison, Benedetto still plays the Cavalcanti prince, sure that a secret protector will rescue him. His visitor is Bertuccio, the count's steward and his own foster-father, who promises to tell him the next day who his real father is.
details: The “Lions' Den” is the section of La Force prison that holds the most dangerous inmates. Andrea, his fine clothes torn but carefully brushed, begs a keeper for twenty francs and boasts of his millionaire relatives. The keeper laughs and lets the convicts close in to beat up “the prince.” Andrea saves himself with a secret bandits' sign that Caderousse taught him, and the convicts accept him as one of their own.

Then he is called to the visitors' room. He has stayed silent since his arrest, convinced that the powerful protector who gave him money, a noble father and a brilliant marriage will save him, and he does not want to offend that person. The visitor is Bertuccio, who greets him as “Benedetto” and “unhappy child” and arranges for them to talk in a private room.

Andrea calls Bertuccio his adopted father. But he insists that someone else gave him 100,000 francs, invented an Italian father for him, and got him invited to the dinner at Auteuil, and he hints that his real father must be the Count of Monte Cristo. Bertuccio sternly forbids him to say so: the count is too favoured by Heaven to have such a son. Andrea has fallen into “terrible hands,” he warns, hands that can save him or crush him. Andrea demands to know his father, and Bertuccio says that is why he came. Just then the examining magistrate (the judge who questions suspects before trial) sends for the prisoner, and Bertuccio promises to return tomorrow.

title: The Judge
summary: On the morning of Benedetto's trial, Villefort confronts his wife with her four murders. To spare his name a public scandal, he orders her to take her own poison before he comes back from court.
details: Ever since the abbé's vigil, Noirtier has been strangely calm. Villefort has replaced every servant and shut himself away to prepare the case against Caderousse's murderer, even though the main evidence is a few words written by a dying convict. Once, in the garden, he sees Noirtier glaring with hatred at Madame de Villefort as she plays with Edward, and then at him, as if reminding him of his oath. “Have patience but one day longer,” Villefort answers.

He works through the night. In the morning his wife sends him a cup of chocolate, and he swallows it in one gulp, almost hoping it is poisoned. It is not. When she asks to come to the trial, he sends word that she should wait for him in her room. There he sends Edward out and bolts the door.

He asks her where she keeps the poison she uses, and accuses her of murdering M. and Madame de Saint-Méran, Barrois and Valentine. She cannot deny it. He reminds her that the scaffold awaits poisoners, but says he will not let his wife dishonour his name and his son. Surely, he says, she has kept some of her deadliest poison for herself. She begs for her life for Edward's sake. He replies that if she lived, she might one day kill the boy too. If he finds her alive when he returns, he warns, she will sleep in prison that night. He says farewell, and as she faints he double-locks the door behind him.

title: The Assizes
summary: All fashionable Paris crowds into the court for Benedetto's trial. While they wait, Beauchamp, Debray and Château-Renaud gossip about the deaths at Villefort's house, the absent count, and a veiled lady who looks like Madame Danglars.
details: “The Benedetto affair” is the sensation of Paris. Many who knew the charming “Prince Cavalcanti” think he must be the victim of some plot, and some expect his father to reappear. On a brilliant September day the courtroom fills early.

Debray reports that the president of the court thinks Benedetto is just a commonplace rascal. Beauchamp spots a veiled lady he is sure is Madame Danglars, only ten days after her daughter's flight and three after her husband's bankruptcy. Debray blushes and says she is probably some foreign princess. They notice Madame de Villefort is not there. Debray likes her, while Château-Renaud dislikes her by instinct.

Beauchamp repeats a story from a servant who left Villefort's house: little Edward has supposedly been poisoning anyone who displeased him, using a drug from his mother's laboratory. The others call it absurd. Debray says the count is keeping out of sight because the Cavalcantis tricked him out of 100,000 francs. Beauchamp points out that the count is involved anyway: Caderousse was killed as he left the count's house, and the bloodstained waistcoat holding the letter that stopped the marriage contract lies on the evidence table. Château-Renaud has called on Morrel three times without seeing him. Then the court enters.

title: The Indictment
summary: At his trial Benedetto reveals that he was born at Auteuil in 1817 and buried alive by his father, and that his father is the prosecutor himself, M. de Villefort. Villefort, broken, admits it before the court and walks out, and Madame Danglars faints in the crowd.
details: Villefort's indictment is powerful, but Benedetto stays calm and stares straight back at him. Asked his name, he asks to answer the questions in his own order. He gives his age: born on the night of 27 September 1817. He gives his birthplace: Auteuil. Villefort turns livid. As for his profession, he was a forger, then a thief, and lately an assassin.

He cannot give his own name, he says, but he can give his father's: the king's attorney, Villefort. The court erupts. He explains that he was born at No. 28 Rue de la Fontaine in a room hung with red damask. His father told his mother the baby was dead, wrapped him in a napkin marked with an H and an N, and buried him alive in the garden. A man with a vendetta against his father stabbed him, dug up the box and took the living baby to the foundling hospital. Later a woman from Rogliano in Corsica claimed him. The reader knows these two from Bertuccio's own story: Bertuccio and his sister-in-law Assunta. His adopted father once told him the crime was his father's, not his.

Asked about his mother, Benedetto says she thought him dead and is innocent. A veiled lady in the crowd shrieks and is carried out; her veil falls, and it is Madame Danglars. When the president demands proof, Benedetto says, “Look at M. de Villefort.” Villefort staggers forward, says no proof is needed, admits that everything is true and that he is “in the hands of an avenging God,” and leaves, placing himself under the authority of whoever succeeds him. The case is adjourned, and Benedetto leaves calm and more fascinating than ever.

title: Expiation
summary: Villefort rushes home meaning to save his wife and flee with her, but finds that she has poisoned herself and taken Edward with her. The Abbé Busoni, visiting Noirtier, reveals himself as Edmond Dantès. Villefort shows him the bodies and loses his mind.
details: The crowd parts silently for Villefort. In his carriage, his wife's forgotten fan reminds him of the sentence he passed on her. Now that his own guilt is public, he decides she must live: they will flee together, she will repent and raise Edward, and no one will know her crimes. He orders the coachman to hurry.

Edward's room is empty and his wife's door is bolted. Villefort breaks it open. Héloïse stands rigid, says “It is done,” and falls dead, clutching a crystal bottle. The servants say she sent for Edward half an hour ago. Beyond her body Villefort finds the boy on a sofa, dead, with a note in her hand: “A good mother cannot depart without her son.”

Shattered, Villefort goes down to his father and finds the Abbé Busoni there. The abbé says Villefort has paid his debt and that he will pray for him. Then he pulls off his wig, and Villefort sees the Count of Monte Cristo. The count tells him to go back further, to his wedding day in Marseilles twenty-three years ago: “I am Edmond Dantès!” Villefort drags him upstairs to the bodies and cries, “Are you well avenged?”

The count turns pale, feeling that he has gone beyond the bounds of vengeance. He carries Edward into Valentine's old room and tries for a quarter of an hour to revive him, but no skill can do it. He lays the boy beside his mother. Outside, Villefort is digging wildly in the garden, crying that he will find the child: he has gone mad. Doubting for the first time whether he had the right to do what he did, the count resolves to “save the last.” He leaves Paris with Morrel the next day. Haydée has gone ahead with Ali, and Bertuccio stays behind with Noirtier.

title: The Departure
summary: The count says goodbye to Julie and Emmanuel and leaves Paris with Maximilian. In Marseilles they see Albert sail for Africa, and the count visits Mercédès in old Dantès' house for a last, sorrowful talk.
details: Julie and Emmanuel talk about the sudden falls of Morcerf, Danglars and Villefort, as if some avenging spirit were at work. The count arrives to collect Maximilian. They will go first to Marseilles, and he must be in Rome in five days. He tells his friends they will probably never see him again, and as he leaves he asks Julie whether she still trusts “Sinbad the Sailor.” Outside, Ali reports that he placed the count's letter before Noirtier, who signalled “yes.”

From the hill of Villejuif the count looks back over Paris and declares his mission complete. He says he leaves without pride or hatred, though with many regrets. They travel swiftly by carriage and steamboat to Marseilles. On the quay where Morrel's father once greeted the Pharaon, they see Albert, now in uniform, sailing for Algiers, while a veiled woman waves goodbye. Morrel goes to visit his father's grave.

The count goes to the little house in the Allées de Meilhan, his father's old home, which he has given to Mercédès. He finds her weeping in the garden. He admits he caused her misfortunes, but she cannot hate the man who spared her son. Instead she blames herself: she was weak, she married Fernand, and she let him die. The count says he was only an instrument of God, driven on like an avenging angel. She asks only for Albert's happiness and refuses money for herself, saying she will live on the sum he left buried in the garden and spend her days in prayer. She promises they will meet again in heaven. Alone at the window, she murmurs, “Edmond, Edmond, Edmond!”

title: The Past
summary: Shaken by doubt, the count revisits the Château d'If, hears his own story told as legend, and regains his conviction when he finds the Abbé Faria's manuscript. He then arranges to meet Maximilian on the island of Monte Cristo on 5 October.
details: Since Edward's death the count has feared that his vengeance went astray. To look his past in the face, he hires a boat to the Château d'If, retracing the journey he made as a prisoner twenty-four years ago. The fortress has held no prisoners since the revolution of 1830.

A guide shows him his old cell and tells a local legend: a dangerous prisoner dug a tunnel to the cell of a “mad” priest, took the dead priest's place in his burial sack, and was thrown into the sea, surely to drown. He was known only as “No. 34.” Alone in the dark, the count finds the marks of his old despair and the words he scratched on the wall: “Oh, God! preserve my memory!” In Faria's cell, No. 27, he weeps. The guide sells him Faria's great manuscript, written on strips of cloth. Its epigraph, “Thou shalt tear out the dragons' teeth, and shall trample the lions under foot, saith the Lord,” seems an answer to his doubts. He gives the guide 10,000 francs. Passing the Catalans on the way back, he murmurs a woman's name, and it is Haydée's.

At the cemetery he finds Morrel by his parents' graves. The count never found his own father's grave. He tells Morrel about a man who lost his father and his bride and spent fourteen years in a dungeon. That man's father died in poverty, and his bride married one of his persecutors, yet he has found peace and hopes to be happy. Morrel renews his promise. The count tells him that a yacht, the Eurus, will wait at Bastia on 4 October to bring him to the island of Monte Cristo on the 5th. Then the count leaves by steamer for Italy.

title: Peppino
summary: Danglars reaches Rome and cashes the count's receipt at Thomson & French, unaware that the bandit Peppino is shadowing him. Leaving the city, he is kidnapped and taken to Luigi Vampa's hideout in the catacombs of Saint Sebastian.
details: A Frenchman wearing the ribbon of the Legion of Honour, who knows no Italian beyond musical terms like “Allegro!” and “Moderato!”, arrives in Rome and checks in at Signor Pastrini's hotel. It is Danglars. A man follows him to the bank of Thomson & French. This is Peppino, and the bank clerk is clearly in league with the bandits. They had been told in advance that Danglars was coming to draw about five million francs on the Count of Monte Cristo's receipt.

Danglars leaves delighted, with a letter of credit in his pocketbook, and sleeps with it under his pillow. Next afternoon he sets off on the Ancona road, planning to collect his money in Venice and Vienna. He dozes off. At a stop, fresh horses are harnessed, and a strong hand pushes him back when he tries to get out. Riders gallop on both sides, and a voice orders, “Dentro la testa!” (Heads in!). At first he fears he has been arrested. Then he realizes they have circled back past Rome onto the Appian Way.

Forced out of the carriage, he is led by Peppino through tall weeds into a hole in the rock and along the catacombs to the bandit chief, who is reading Plutarch's Life of Alexander. Danglars recognizes Luigi Vampa from Albert's stories, and he is locked in the same cell Albert once occupied. Since they have not killed him, he reasons, they mean to ransom him, perhaps for 8,000 crowns, twice Albert's price, leaving him over five million. Comforted, he falls asleep.

title: Luigi Vampa’s Bill of Fare
summary: Danglars wakes to find his money untouched, but his captors will sell him food only at outrageous prices: a hundred thousand francs for a chicken. Starving, he signs a draft on his own fortune.
details: Danglars wakes and finds his purse and his letter of credit for 5,050,000 francs untouched. Puzzled by these “singular bandits,” he decides to wait for them to make the first move. Hours pass with no food. Through the cracks in the door he watches his guards eat bread, cheese and onions, which start to look surprisingly appetizing. When he asks the giant red-haired guard for dinner, the man ignores him.

Then Peppino comes on duty with a pan of chickpeas and bacon, a basket of grapes and a flask of Orvieto wine. He politely offers Danglars anything he wants, as long as he pays. A youth brings in a roast fowl on a silver dish. Danglars tosses down a louis (a gold coin worth 20 francs), but Peppino says he still owes 4,999 more, a total of 100,000 francs. Danglars thinks it is a joke and refuses, and the fowl is taken away.

Half an hour later he asks for dry bread. It costs the same, Peppino explains, because they have “a fixed price for all our provisions.” When Danglars protests that he does not carry 100,000 francs, Peppino reminds him that he carries 5,050,000, enough for fifty fowls and a half. At last Danglars understands. He writes a draft on Thomson & French and eats a chicken that seems very thin for its price.

title: The Pardon
summary: Vampa tells Danglars that his ransom is all five million, and that a higher chief forbids killing him. Starved until he repents, Danglars is confronted by the count, who reveals himself as Edmond Dantès, forgives him, and sets him free.
details: The next day Danglars is thirsty. Wine is 25,000 francs a bottle, and water is “even more scarce.” He demands to see the chief. Vampa tells him the ransom is simply the five million he carries, and that they are forbidden to shed his blood by a chief above Vampa himself. Danglars swears he will never sign again, but after two days he pays a million for a supper.

Twelve days later, after many splendid meals, he has only 50,000 francs left. Suddenly he clings to that last sum and chooses hunger instead. He prays and weeps for the first time in years. In his delirium he sees an old man dying of hunger on a pallet. By the fifth day he is chewing the matting on the floor. He crawls to the door and begs Vampa to take his last gold and just let him live.

Vampa answers that others have suffered more: men who died of hunger. A man in a cloak asks Danglars whether he repents, and Danglars says he does. The man steps into the light. He is not the Count of Monte Cristo, he says, but Edmond Dantès, whom Danglars sold and dishonoured, and whose father Danglars condemned to starve. He forgives Danglars and lets him keep the 50,000 francs. The five million Danglars stole from the hospitals has been returned to them by an unknown hand. Of Danglars' accomplices, he says, one is mad and the other dead. Danglars is fed and left free by the roadside. At dawn he bends over a stream to drink and sees that his hair has turned completely white.

title: The Fifth of October
summary: On 5 October Maximilian comes to Monte Cristo to die. The count gives him what seems a deadly drug, but as he sinks, Valentine appears, alive. Haydée confesses her love, and the count leaves the young couple his fortune and a farewell letter and sails away with her.
details: At sunset Maximilian's yacht reaches the island. He wades ashore, and the count greets him. Morrel is calm and still determined to die: he waited and hoped for a month, in vain. In the underground palace the count offers him nearly a hundred million francs to live, but Morrel holds him to his word. At half past eleven the count gives him a greenish substance from a jewelled golden box. Morrel stops the count from taking some himself, swallows it, and feels himself slipping away, promising to tell Valentine what the count has done for him.

As his sight fades, a door opens and a beautiful young woman appears. It is Valentine, alive. The count tells her that Morrel chose death to find her, and that he himself has “vanquished death.” He hopes God will accept the saving of these two lives as his atonement. Valentine speaks of Haydée, whom she loves as a sister, and the count asks her to protect Haydée, whom he means to free tomorrow and restore to her father's name and riches. Haydée overhears. She says she would die without him and confesses that she loves him. The count accepts her love as God's pardon and leads her away.

An hour later Morrel revives. Thinking the count has cheated him, he reaches for a knife, and then he sees Valentine. At dawn, walking by the sea, she tells him how the count revealed the crime and let her fake her death. Jacopo, the yacht's captain, brings a letter. Noirtier waits in Leghorn (Livorno) to bless their marriage. The grotto, the house in the Champs-Élysées and the château at Tréport are wedding gifts from Edmond Dantès, and he asks Valentine to give her father's fortune to the poor. The letter also tells her, for the first time, that her father is mad and her brother dead. It ends: all human wisdom is summed up in two words, “Wait and hope.” On the horizon, a white sail carries the count and Haydée away.
